name: Patellofemoral Pain
summary: Peripatellar or retropatellar pain aggravated by loaded knee flexion such as stairs, squatting, running or prolonged sitting.

looksLike: Pain with stairs, squat, running or prolonged sitting
redFlags: Large acute effusion or traumatic onset
Fever/hot joint or inability to weight bear
firstSteps: Explain load-capacity relationship and adjust painful running/jumping temporarily
Begin knee and/or hip strengthening at manageable range
selfCare: Reduce only the aggravating load temporarily, not all activity
Use pain-monitoring to guide training volume

assess: Possible hip/knee strength or movement-control deficits
Patellar mobility is variable and not diagnostic alone
Pain with squat, stairs, running or prolonged sitting

tests.name: Single-Leg Squat
tests.purpose: Assess functional load tolerance and movement strategy while reproducing familiar anterior knee pain.
tests.positive: Familiar peripatellar pain during loaded knee flexion.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Explain load-capacity relationship and adjust painful running/jumping temporarily
Begin knee and/or hip strengthening at manageable range
dose: Isometric quadriceps or shallow squat: 4–5 x 20–30 seconds
Temporarily reduce provoking volume, not all activity
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Add step-down, squat and single-leg control
Use running retraining only when relevant to individual deficits
dose: Hip abductor/external rotator strengthening: 2–3 x 10–15, 2–3 days/week
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Graded return to running, jumping and stairs
Progress volume, speed and hills separately
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Quadriceps and hip capacity appropriate for goals

logic: The main problem is often load tolerance rather than a patella that must be permanently 'realigned'.
Treat the whole kinetic chain when relevant, especially knee extensor and hip capacity.
Use taping/manual therapy as short-term pain reducers to allow better exercise.
structures: Patellofemoral joint and surrounding tissues; pain is multifactorial and not necessarily due to maltracking.
mechanism: Reduced capacity relative to running, jumping or squat demand
Multiple individual biomechanical and contextual contributors
classification: Assess coexisting instability, cartilage injury or patellar tendinopathy
investigations: Usually clinical; imaging not routinely needed for typical PFP.
Radiographs/MRI if trauma, recurrent instability, large effusion, locking or atypical persistent symptoms.
manual: Patellar taping or mobilisation may provide short-term adjunctive relief in selected patients.
Manual therapy should not replace hip and knee exercise.
Patellar mobilization when restricted and symptom-relevant
MWM or taping as a pain-reduction strategy during exercise
Patellar mobilization is only indicated if there is a relevant mobility deficit.
A pain-reducing MWM or taping strategy can be used during squat/step and then gradually withdrawn as capacity improves.
modalities: Foot orthoses may help selected patients short term when matched to response.
Routine passive electrotherapy is not a core intervention.
Ice after provocative activity if preferred
TENS is rarely necessary but may be used briefly for pain
Passive modalities are not primary care
Cold can be used for comfort after activity.
Passive electrotherapy is not required in routine management.
dosing: Calf/foot work when relevant: 2–3 sets × 10–20 reps.
Return-to-running exposure: increase only one variable at a time.
progression: Increase knee flexion depth and external load
Progress to hopping, running and sport-specific change of direction
Allow mild pain during exercise if it remains acceptable and settles by the next day.
Progress depth, load, speed and single-leg demand gradually.
Return to jumping/running after basic strength and step control improve.
mistakes: Focusing on static knee valgus as the diagnosis
Blaming every case on VMO weakness.
Keeping the patient in low-load band exercises for months.
pearls: Combined hip- and knee-targeted exercise is supported by the PFP guideline.
Use the patient's pain response and functional goals to select exercise range.
education: Explain load tolerance in simple terms: the knee usually needs better capacity, not permanent avoidance.
Normalize gradual exposure to stairs, squats and running.
Use pain-monitoring rather than fear-based restriction.
escalation: Further medical assessment for recurrent effusion, locking or failure to improve with a well-adhered rehabilitation plan

tests.name: Single-Leg Squat
tests.purpose: Assess functional load tolerance and movement strategy while reproducing familiar anterior knee pain.
tests.positive: Familiar peripatellar pain during loaded knee flexion.
tests.patientPosition: Patient stands on one leg near support and performs controlled shallow-to-deeper squat; observe pelvis, trunk and knee.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Supports load-related PFP when history fits; movement appearance alone does not diagnose cause.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
